p.x:
I have a pink piggy bank in my bedroom. Every week, I put half of my pocket money in it. When I get birthday money from my grandma, I put it in too. Sometimes, she gives me a banknote, not coins!
My dad works in an office. On payday, he gives me a little extra. At New Year, he gets a bonus from his company. He says, "I never buy lottery tickets. Saving is better!"
Last month, I opened my piggy bank and counted the money. The total was 2,000 baht! I want to buy a new bike.

Learning to manage money is an important life skill. The first step is to know the difference between what is essential, like food, rent and transport, and what is not. Many people waste money on small things every day, such as snacks and coffee, without noticing.
A good habit is to save a little every month. Open a savings account at a bank, and use mobile banking to check how much you spend. Some people keep their bank card at home so they can't spend too much when they go out.
It's also important to be careful when you borrow. If a friend lends you money, pay them back quickly. Being generous is good, but you shouldn't spend so much that you end up broke at the end of the month. On the other hand, nobody likes someone who is stingy and never pays for anything!
When you start work, you may hope for a pay rise every year. But even if you earn more, it's wise to keep saving. Many wealthy people became rich not because they had high salaries, but because they spent less than they earned.

Financial experts often say that the key to long-term security is not how much you earn, but what you do with it. One of the most powerful forces in personal finance is compound interest, in which interest is earned not only on the original savings but also on the interest already added. Over decades, even small regular contributions can grow into a substantial nest egg.
Many people try to increase their wealth by investing in the stock market. Buying shares makes you a part-owner of a company, and some firms pay a dividend to shareholders from their profits. However, share prices can rise and fall sharply, so advisers recommend that investors diversify, spreading their money across different types of investment. A balanced portfolio might include shares, bonds and property. An asset such as a flat can also generate passive income through rent.
Yet many young people struggle to make ends meet, let alone invest. Rising living costs mean that some must tighten their belts or take on a side hustle to supplement their income. Buy now, pay later schemes, which allow consumers to spread the cost of purchases over several instalments, have become extremely popular, but critics warn that they encourage people to spend beyond their means and can damage a person's credit score if payments are missed.
This is why many educators argue that financial literacy should be taught in schools. Understanding how to live within your means, set a financial goal and avoid the temptation to gamble could protect young people from serious debt. Being well-off is not simply about income or net worth. Even an unexpected windfall can disappear quickly without good habits, while a bargain hunter on a modest salary may live very comfortably.
